sections.title: Executive Summary
sections.content: Artificial Intelligence is expected to contribute between $500 billion and $540 billion to the Indian economy by 2025 [E1][E2]. Projections indicate that nearly 20 million new jobs could be created by 2025 [E3][E4]. However, automation poses risks, with estimates suggesting up to 60 million workers in the manufacturing sector could be displaced by 2030 [E5].

sections.title: Market Insights
sections.content: The Indian market faces significant shifts due to Artificial Intelligence, with approximately 25% of the workforce in occupations exposed to this technology [E6]. In urban India, nearly half of all jobs are exposed to AI-related changes [E7]. Furthermore, AI is expected to impact about 300 million blue-collar workers in the country [E8].

sections.title: Competitor Analysis
sections.content: The accepted evidence does not identify enough verified companies providing products or services in the Artificial Intelligence and Employment market to support a company-level competitor comparison. Funding and investor activity may provide market context, but do not establish that an organisation is a competitor.

sections.title: Opportunities and Risks
sections.content:
Opportunities:
• The expansion of the semiconductor market in India is projected to reach $110 billion by 2030 and is expected to create one million jobs by 2026 [E9][E10].
• Government and industry collaborations, such as the YUVAI program launched by the National e-Governance Division and Intel India, aim to provide school students with essential AI skills [E11][E12].
• Employers are increasingly prioritizing skills over formal education, as evidenced by a 36 percent increase in job postings in India that do not require a specific degree between 2024 and 2026 [E13].
Risks:
• A potential white-collar recession is anticipated in India by 2027, with 67.5% of engineers reporting that their jobs are already being negatively impacted by AI [E14][E15].
• The Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023 has been criticized for neglecting challenges related to algorithmic labour management, workplace monitoring, and gig economy insecurity (verify the current status) [E16].
• India reports the highest cybercrime rate in the world, which is thirty percent above the global average, presenting a significant challenge for the digital workforce [E17].

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.content:
• Prioritize upskilling programs for engineers, as 87.5% of them believe such training is critical to safeguarding their careers against technological disruption [E18].
• Develop targeted transition support for the manufacturing sector, given that automation could displace up to 60 million workers by 2030 [E5].
• Focus on roles that do not require specific degrees, as job postings of this nature increased by 36 percent between 2024 and 2026 [E13].

sections.content:

sections.title: Glossary
sections.content:
Simple explanations of important terms used in this report. These definitions are explanatory notes, not research evidence.
- Artificial Intelligence: This refers to computer systems capable of performing tasks that typically require human intelligence.
- Automation: This is the use of technology to perform tasks with minimal human intervention.
- Blue-collar workers: These are employees who perform manual labor in industrial or manufacturing settings.
- Semiconductor: This is a material used in electronic devices to control the flow of electrical current.
- White-collar recession: This describes a period of significant job losses or economic decline specifically affecting professional and office-based roles.
- Algorithmic labour management: This involves using software and data analysis to oversee and direct the work of employees.
- Gig economy: This is a labor market characterized by the prevalence of short-term contracts or freelance work.
- Upskilling: This is the process of teaching employees new skills to improve their performance or prepare them for different roles.
- Technological disruption: This refers to significant changes in industries or markets caused by the introduction of new technologies.
